description: Equipo SPACE MAKER LAZALA, es un grupo de estudiantes del Politécnico Mercedes María Lazala, en República Dominicana, que participa en el concurso de la NASA con el desarrollo de un simulador interactivo del cohete Artemis II. Nuestro proyecto busca acercar la exploración espacial a estudiantes de habla hispana, representando de forma visual y comprensible las etapas de la misión: lanzamiento, órbita terrestre, viaje a la Luna, sobrevuelo lunar y regreso a la Tierra.
summary: We developed the Artemis II Simulator, an interactive space mission trainer designed for the global challenge Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer at the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project combines interactive digital environments, 3D modeling and additive manufacturing of a spacecraft and its launch pad, alongside Arduino-based embedded electronic systems. The solution addresses the limitations of traditional passive teaching through an experiential "learning by doing" methodology, where children aged 7 to 12 assume the role of commanders of a lunar or Martian base. They must monitor and balance critical survival variables—such as oxygen, power, radiation, food, and telecommunications—through a physical console and digital simulation.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Our project is an interactive simulation platform of the Artemis II mission that allows users to experience, step by step, NASA's first crewed flight around the Moon in over 50 years. Through an immersive interface and gamification dynamics (minigames and real-time decision-making), players take on the role of the crew and mission control: from the launch of the SLS rocket and trans-lunar injection maneuvers, to the lunar flyby and safe reentry into Earth's atmosphere. Each phase integrates real trajectory data, basic telemetry, and problem-solving challenges (such as oxygen management, course correction, and communications) that require applying real scientific principles to successfully complete the mission.

What benefits does it have?

Democratization of space knowledge: Transforms complex concepts of astrophysics, aerospace engineering, and orbital mechanics into accessible, visual, and understandable experiences for students and the general public.

Active and practical learning: Fosters critical thinking, problem-solving under pressure, and curiosity for STEM careers (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics) through direct experimentation.

Versatile pedagogical tool: Serves as a dynamic educational resource for teachers and educational centers seeking to teach space exploration in a modern and interactive way without the need for expensive equipment.

What is the anticipated impact of the project?

The project seeks to inspire the next generation of explorers, scientists, and engineers, bringing the Artemis program closer to educational communities and young people in Spanish-speaking countries and around the world. In the short term, we hope to increase interest and understanding of the scientific objectives of Artemis II and sustainable human presence on the Moon. In the medium and long term, we aspire for the platform to be adopted as support material in classrooms and scientific workshops, sparking technological vocations and strengthening scientific culture.

Hardware and collaboration: Standard laptops, version control tools, and cloud collaborative platforms for project design, testing, and documentation.

How is your project creative?

Instead of presenting the Artemis II mission as a simple passive animation or informative text, we combine the scientific rigor of NASA data with educational video game mechanics. We turn real technical milestones—such as engine ignition or temporary loss of signal behind the far side of the Moon—into interactive challenges where the user not only observes history, but stars in it and understands the physical consequences of each decision.

What factors did your team take into account?

Scientific and educational accuracy: Ensuring that mission phases, terminology, and challenges faithfully reflect the actual architecture of Artemis II.

Accessibility and inclusiveness: Designing an intuitive, visually appealing, and easy-to-use interface on conventional devices, without requiring advanced prior knowledge or high-end hardware.

User experience (UX) and gameplay: Achieving a balance between technical rigor and fun, maintaining user interest through clear feedback and dynamic progression.

Scalability: Structuring the project modularly so that new program missions (such as Artemis III and the lunar landing) can be added in the future.
